input: what's that counter thing from dijkstra that you can use both as a lock and for making a thread wait on something?
expected_output: It is a semaphore: an object holding an integer value that you manipulate with two routines, which in POSIX are sem_wait() and sem_post(). Dijkstra and colleagues invented it as a single primitive for all synchronization, so it can act as both a lock and a condition variable.

evidence.quote: Indeed, Dijkstra and colleagues invented the semaphore as a single primitive for all things related to synchronization; as you will see, one can use semaphores as both locks and condition variables.
A semaphore is an object with an integer value that we can manipulate with two routines; in the POSIX standard, these routines are sem wait() and sem post()

input: whats it called when a semaphore stands in for a mutex, and why that name?
expected_output: It is called a binary semaphore. The name comes from the fact that a lock only has two states, held and not held.

evidence.quote: Because locks only have two states (held and not held), we sometimes call a semaphore used as a lock a binary semaphore.

input: why does a semaphore guarding a critical section have to be set up with 1 instead of 0?
expected_output: With an initial value of 1, the first thread to call sem_wait() decrements the value to 0. Since it waits only if the value is less than 0, it simply returns and the thread is free to enter the critical section. That is why the initial value for a lock should be 1. If the semaphore started at 0, the first thread's sem_wait() would decrement it to -1 and that thread would wait even though no one holds the lock, so no thread could ever enter the critical section.

evidence.quote: Looking back at definition of the sem wait() and sem post() routines above, we can see that the initial value should be 1.
it will first decrement the value of the semaphore, changing it to 0. Then, it will wait only if the value is not greater than or equal to 0.
Because the value is 0, sem wait() will simply return and the calling thread will continue; Thread 0 is now free to enter the critical section.
decrement the value of semaphore s by one 3 wait if value of semaphore s is negative

input: when the main thread spawns a worker and blocks on a semaphore until the worker finishes, why initialize it to 0?
expected_output: If the parent calls sem_wait() before the child has posted, we want the parent to wait, which only happens if the value is not greater than 0, so 0 is the initial value. If the child finishes first, its sem_post() raises the value from 0 to 1, so when the parent later calls sem_wait() it finds 1, decrements to 0 and returns without waiting. Either order gives the desired effect.

evidence.quote: the parent will call sem wait() before the child has called sem post(); we’d like the parent to wait for the child to run. The only way this will happen is if the value of the semaphore is not greater than 0; hence, 0 is the initial value.
the child will first call sem post(), thus incrementing the value of the semaphore from 0 to 1.
the parent will thus decrement the value (to 0) and return from sem wait() without waiting, also achieving the desired effect.

input: my bounded buffer with semaphores locks the mutex before waiting for data or space and sometimes freezes, why?
expected_output: It can deadlock. If the consumer runs first, takes the mutex, and then blocks waiting for data, it still holds the lock. The producer could supply data, but its first step is waiting for the mutex, so each is stuck waiting on the other. The fix is to put the mutex acquire and release just around the critical section and leave the empty/full waits and signals outside it.

evidence.quote: this call causes the consumer to block and thus yield the CPU; importantly, though, the consumer still holds the lock.
The consumer holds the mutex and is waiting for the someone to signal full. The producer could signal full but is waiting for the mutex.
we simply move the mutex acquire and release to be just around the critical section; the full and empty wait and signal code is left outside.

input: bounded buffer w/ semaphores works with 1 slot but w/ 10 slots and several producers i lose data. wats going on
expected_output: With more than one slot and multiple producers there is a race in put(). One producer starts filling entry 0 and is interrupted before it increments the fill counter; another producer then also writes into the 0th element and overwrites the old data. The filling of the buffer and the index increment is a critical section, so mutual exclusion is missing.

evidence.quote: Assume producer Pa gets to run first, and just starts to fill the first buffer entry (fill = 0 at line f1). Before Pa gets a chance to increment the fill counter to 1, it is interrupted.
Producer Pb starts to run, and at line f1 it also puts its data into the 0th element of buffer, which means that the old data there is overwritten!
The filling of a buffer and incrementing of the index into the buffer is a critical section, and thus must be guarded carefully.

input: is it harder to implement a condvar on top of a semaphore, or the semaphore on top of a mutex and condvar?
expected_output: Building a semaphore from a lock and a condition variable is fairly straightforward: you need just one lock, one condition variable, and a state variable tracking the value. Going the other way, building locks and condition variables out of semaphores, is a much trickier proposition, and highly experienced programmers who tried it in the Windows environment ran into many bugs.

we use just one lock and one condition variable, plus a state variable to track the value of the semaphore.

is a much trickier proposition. Some highly experienced concurrent programmers tried to do this in the Windows environment, and many different bugs ensued [B04].

input: How do sem_wait() and sem_post() differ in whether the calling thread can be made to block?
expected_output: sem_wait() may block: it returns right away if the semaphore's value was one or higher when called, otherwise the caller suspends until a later post. sem_post() never waits for a condition; it just increments the value and, if a thread is waiting, wakes one of them.

evidence.quote: sem wait() will either return right away (because the value of the semaphore was one or higher when we called sem wait()), or it will cause the caller to suspend execution waiting for a subsequent post.

sem post() does not wait for some particular condition to hold like sem wait() does. Rather, it simply increments the value of the semaphore and then, if there is a thread waiting to be woken, wakes one of them up.

input: lock semaphore starts at 1, A holds it, B and C try to enter. whats the value, how many asleep, and value after A leaves?
expected_output: A holding the lock means the value is 0. B calls sem_wait() and decrements it to -1 and sleeps; C decrements it to -2 and sleeps. When the value is negative it equals the number of waiting threads, so 2 threads are asleep. When A calls sem_post() it increments the value from -2 to -1 and wakes a waiting thread, leaving one still waiting.

evidence.quote: the value of the semaphore, when negative, is equal to the number of waiting threads [D68b].
In this case, Thread 1 will decrement the value of the semaphore to -1, and thus wait (putting itself to sleep and relinquishing the processor).

When Thread 0 runs again, it will eventually call sem post(), incrementing the value of the semaphore back to zero, and then wake the waiting thread (Thread 1), which will then be able to acquire the lock for itself.
Rather, it simply increments the value of the semaphore and then, if there is a thread waiting to be woken, wakes one of them up.

input: In the dining philosophers setup with five philosophers and forks 0 to 4, where left(p) = p and right(p) = (p + 1) % 5, which forks does philosopher 4 pick up, and in what order, in the original version versus the version where it is changed?
expected_output: For p=4, left(4) = 4 and right(4) = (4+1) % 5 = 0. In the original version every philosopher grabs the left fork first and then the right, so philosopher 4 takes fork 4 and then fork 0. In the fixed version philosopher 4 grabs right before left, so it takes fork 0 then fork 4. This breaks the cycle of waiting, so no one can be stuck holding one fork and waiting for another.

evidence.quote: the modulo operator therein handles the one case where the last philosopher (p=4) tries to grab the fork on their right, which is fork 0.
To acquire the forks, we simply grab a “lock” on each one: first the one on the left, and then the one on the right.
Because the last philosopher tries to grab right before left, there is no situation where each philosopher grabs one fork and is stuck waiting for another; the cycle of waiting is broken.

input: sem_init takes 3 args, whats the middle one for since its always 0, and the last one?
expected_output: The first argument is the semaphore, the third argument is the value it is initialized to (here 1). The second argument is 0 in all the book's examples, which means the semaphore is shared between threads in the same process; other usages that synchronize across processes need a different value.

evidence.quote: we declare a semaphore s and initialize it to the value 1 by passing 1 in as the third argument. The second argument to sem init() will be set to 0 in all of the examples we’ll see; this indicates that the semaphore is shared between threads in the same process.
See the man page for details on other usages of semaphores (namely, how they can be used to synchronize access across different processes), which require a different value for that second argument.

input: in the 5 philosophers thing w/ one semaphore per fork, why does everybody get stuck forever?
expected_output: Each philosopher grabs the left fork first and then tries for the right. If every philosopher grabs their left fork before anyone grabs a right one, each holds one fork and waits for another that a neighbor holds, forever. That is a deadlock.

evidence.quote: The problem is deadlock. If each philosopher happens to grab the fork on their left before any philosopher can grab the fork on their right, each will be stuck holding one fork and waiting for another, forever.
all the forks are acquired, and all the philosophers are stuck waiting for a fork that another philosopher possesses.

input: reader-writer locks are built from semaphores so only one reader at a time, like a mutex right?
expected_output: No. Once a reader has acquired the read lock, more readers are allowed to acquire it too, so many readers can be inside at the same time. Only writers are held back, and a thread wanting the write lock has to wait.

evidence.quote: once a reader has acquired a read lock, more readers will be allowed to acquire the read lock too
however, any thread that wishes to acquire the write lock will have to wait until all readers are finished;

input: readers writer locks let lots of threads read at once so theyre always faster right?
expected_output: Not necessarily. Reader-writer locks often add more overhead, especially with more sophisticated implementations, so they may not speed things up compared to simple and fast locking primitives. The book's advice is that they are complex, complex can mean slow, so try the simple and dumb approach first.

evidence.quote: They often add more overhead (especially with more sophisticated implementations), and thus do not end up speeding up performance as compared to just using simple and fast locking primitives
Although something like reader/writer locks sounds cool, they are complex, and complex can mean slow. Thus, always try the simple and dumb approach first.

input: Suppose a reader-writer lock built from semaphores receives a continuous overlapping stream of readers. What problem can arise for a thread waiting to write, and why?
expected_output: The writer can starve. The first reader acquires the writelock semaphore on behalf of all readers, and any thread wanting the write lock has to wait until all readers are finished. With readers constantly arriving, it would be relatively easy for readers to starve writers.

evidence.quote: in that case, the reader also acquires the write lock by calling sem wait() on the writelock semaphore, and then finally releasing the lock by calling sem post().
any thread that wishes to acquire the write lock will have to wait until all readers are finished
In particular, it would be relatively easy for readers to starve writers.
